name: Allometric Equation Calculator
seoDesc: An allometric equation scales a trait as a power of body mass: Y = aM^b. Free allometric equation calculator: enter your values and get predicted value, log₁₀
summary:
An allometric equation scales a trait as a power of body mass: Y = aM^b. It returns predicted value, log₁₀ of the prediction, change for a doubling of mass and predicted surface exponent, and the panel shows all of them at once.

The exponent is the interesting part — 0.75 for metabolic rate, 1 for volume, 0.67 for surface area — and this calculator applies any allometric equation, reports the exponent's meaning and converts between log and linear forms. Press Calculate and the results appear in the grey boxes; after the first press they keep up with every edit, so there is no page to reload. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the Allometric Equation
sections.html:
Y = a × M^b

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
acoefficient, in units of Y per M^b—
bscaling exponent—
Mbody masskg
Ythe trait being predictedtrait units

sections.title: How do I use the Allometric Equation?
sections.html:
Every input sits in the same order the formula is written, so the page reads like the equation.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: coefficient (a) of 3.4, exponent (b) of 0.75, body mass of 70 kg.

Substituting them into the formula gives predicted value of 82.28, log₁₀ of the prediction of 1.92, change for a doubling of mass of 1.68 ×, predicted surface exponent of 0.67.

Those numbers come from the same solver the page runs in your browser, not from an illustration, so typing different inputs moves the answer exactly as the arithmetic says.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
The number on its own is not a judgement. These are the bands most often used when the result is quoted in a paper, a report or a label:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
b ≈ 0.67Surface scalingareas scale slower than volume
b ≈ 0.75Metabolic scalingKleiber's law for metabolic rate
b ≈ 1.0Isometricthe trait scales in proportion to mass

  • An exponent below 1 means the trait grows slower than mass: bigger animals have relatively lower metabolic rates per kilogram.

  • Coefficients are unit-specific — a mouse-to-elephant equation in kg cannot be fed grams.

  • Log–log plots turn the equation into a straight line whose slope is b and intercept is log a, which is how the parameters are actually fitted.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
These are the errors that account for almost every wrong answer people bring to this calculator:

  • Fitting a straight line to untransformed data and calling the slope an exponent.
  • Using a coefficient published in different units.
  • Extrapolating far beyond the size range the equation was fitted over.

faq.a: Metabolic rate scales as mass^0.75, so a tenfold heavier animal uses about 5.6 times the energy.
Because transport networks — blood vessels, tracheae, xylem — constrain how fast resources can reach tissue as body size grows.

faq.q: What does the Allometric Equation actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns predicted value, log₁₀ of the prediction, change for a doubling of mass and predicted surface exponent. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use it with the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit, and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
